title: Thermal & Statistical Physics
subject: Thermal & Statistical
summary: Thermal physics from microscopic counting: entropy and the second law, temperature, pressure and chemical potential as derivatives of entropy, a brief pass over engines and chemical thermodynamics, Boltzmann statistics and partition functions, quantum statistics (Fermi-Dirac, Bose-Einstein, blackbody, Debye), interacting systems and phase transitions, and a graduate unit on ensembles and fluctuations. Follows Schroeder, with Tong for the advanced material.

units.title: Energy and the First Law (brisk review)
units.summary: A fast pass over temperature, the ideal gas, equipartition, heat, work and heat capacity; the chemist already knows the macroscopic version, so the aim is to restate it in the microscopic language used for the rest of the course.

lessons.title: Thermal equilibrium, the ideal gas and equipartition
objectives: Define temperature operationally and state the zeroth law.
Derive the ideal gas law from kinetic theory, and compute the rms speed of molecules at a given temperature.
State the equipartition theorem and use it to predict internal energy and heat capacities of monatomic and diatomic gases, naming which degrees of freedom are frozen out at room temperature.
Explain why the observed C_V of H2 steps with temperature, in terms of rotational and vibrational energy-level spacings (a quantum effect you will derive later).

lectures.title: Statistical Physics I course page (lecture notes, problem sets, exams)

demoIdeas: Gas of hard spheres in a box with a temperature slider: histogram of speeds, pressure from wall impacts, and the PV=NkT line.

lessons.title: Heat, work and compression
objectives: State the first law and distinguish heat from work as two modes of energy transfer.
Compute the work done on an ideal gas in isothermal, adiabatic, isobaric and isochoric quasistatic processes.
Derive the adiabatic relation PV^gamma = const from the first law and equipartition.
Explain what quasistatic means and why it matters for evaluating W = -integral P dV.
demoIdeas: Interactive PV diagram: draw isothermal/adiabatic/isobaric paths between two states and see Q, W and Delta U for each.

lessons.title: Heat capacity, enthalpy and latent heat
objectives: Define C_V and C_P and relate them for an ideal gas (C_P - C_V = Nk).
Define enthalpy and compute heat transferred at constant pressure, including latent heat in a phase change.
Extract a heat capacity from a measured temperature rise and use it to estimate energy changes.

units.title: The Second Law and Entropy
units.summary: Entropy as the logarithm of the number of microstates: counting for two-state systems, Einstein solids and ideal gases, why large systems behave irreversibly, and the Sackur-Tetrode entropy.

lessons.title: Two-state systems and the Einstein solid
objectives: Compute multiplicities of a collection of two-state systems (coins or spins) and of an Einstein solid with q quanta and N oscillators using binomial counting.
State the fundamental assumption of statistical mechanics (all accessible microstates equally likely in an isolated system) and the definition of macrostate versus microstate.
Define entropy S = k ln Omega and compute it for a simple system.
Relate this counting to everyday chemistry: the number of microstates of a population of NMR spin-1/2 nuclei in a field.

readings.title: The Einstein Model of a Solid

lectures.title: Lecture 1: Entropy and conservation of information

demoIdeas: Coin-flip and Einstein-solid multiplicity explorer: choose N and q, see Omega, the most probable macrostate and its narrow peak.

lessons.title: Interacting systems and large systems
objectives: Compute the multiplicity of two Einstein solids sharing energy and find the most probable energy partition.
Use Stirling's approximation and Gaussian approximation to the multiplicity function to show that the peak width scales as 1/sqrt(N).
Explain why macroscopic systems relax to equilibrium irreversibly in terms of overwhelming probability, not impossibility.
demoIdeas: Two Einstein solids exchanging quanta: live plot of Omega_A Omega_B versus q_A for increasing N, showing the peak narrowing.

lessons.title: The ideal gas: multiplicity and the Sackur-Tetrode equation
objectives: Count the states of a single particle in a box and an N-particle ideal gas, including the factor 1/N! for identical particles.
Derive the Sackur-Tetrode equation for the entropy of a monatomic ideal gas.
Use it to compute the entropy change of free expansion and of mixing, identifying the Gibbs paradox.
Compute an absolute entropy of a gas such as argon at 298 K and compare with the tabulated standard molar entropy.

lectures.title: MB, ED & BE Statistics and Sackur-Tetrode equation

lectures.source: Suresh Govindarajan (IIT Madras): Lectures on Statistical Physics
lectures.title: Lecture 5: Ideal Gas (Part 2 of 2)

lessons.title: Entropy and the second law
objectives: State the second law in its statistical form and as dS >= 0 for isolated systems.
Calculate entropy changes for reversible and irreversible processes (heating, expansion, mixing) and show that total entropy increases for the irreversible ones.
Explain the relation of entropy to information and why a microscopic reversible dynamics still yields an arrow of time.
Use S = integral C_V dT / T to compute entropy changes from measured heat capacities.
demoIdeas: Gas free-expansion with N particles: histogram of the left-half fraction over time showing return to equilibrium and rare fluctuations for small N.

units.title: Interactions and Implications: Temperature, Pressure, Chemical Potential
units.summary: Defining temperature, pressure and chemical potential as derivatives of entropy; paramagnet as a worked microscopic example; the thermodynamic identity.

lessons.title: Temperature as a derivative of entropy
objectives: Derive 1/T = (dS/dU) from the requirement that two systems exchanging energy maximise total multiplicity.
Compute T(U) for the Einstein solid and for an ideal gas and recover U = (3/2)NkT.
Explain negative temperatures in a bounded-spectrum spin system.
Determine entropy from measured heat capacities using the relation dS = C dT/T and the third-law convention S(0)=0.
demoIdeas: Entropy-vs-energy curves for two systems brought into contact; the common-slope condition for equilibrium.

lessons.title: The paramagnet
objectives: Compute the entropy, temperature and magnetization of a two-state paramagnet as functions of energy using multiplicity.
Derive the Curie law at high temperature and the saturation at low temperature.
Connect the model to NMR: Boltzmann polarisation of spin-1/2 nuclei in a field and why NMR signal grows as B/T.
Explain the meaning of negative temperature for this system.
demoIdeas: Spin paramagnet: B and T sliders, spin up/down population bar, M(B/T) curve with Curie limit.

lessons.title: Mechanical equilibrium and pressure
objectives: Derive P/T = (dS/dV) from entropy maximisation for two systems exchanging volume.
State the thermodynamic identity dU = T dS - P dV and derive PV = NkT from the entropy of an ideal gas.
Use the identity to compute reversible heat and work for a process described by S(U,V).

lectures.title: Lecture 5: Pressure of an ideal gas and fluctuations

lessons.title: Diffusive equilibrium and the chemical potential
objectives: Define the chemical potential mu = -T (dS/dN) and derive the equality of mu between systems in diffusive equilibrium.
Write the full thermodynamic identity dU = T dS - P dV + mu dN.
Compute mu for the ideal gas from the Sackur-Tetrode equation and interpret its dependence on concentration and temperature.
Explain why mu is the quantity that governs chemical equilibrium and phase coexistence (the chemist's partial molar Gibbs energy).

lectures.source: IIT Bombay / Prof. Nitin Kumar: Thermal and Statistical Physics (SWAYAM Prabha)
lectures.title: Chemical Potential and its Thermodynamics Significance

demoIdeas: Two chambers exchanging particles: mu on each side versus density and the approach to equal mu.

units.title: Engines, Free Energy and Chemical Thermodynamics (brief)
units.summary: Carnot limits, Helmholtz and Gibbs free energy as the quantities minimised at equilibrium, phase transformations and chemical equilibrium; mostly a restatement of the chemist's physical chemistry in the new language.

lessons.title: Heat engines, Carnot efficiency and refrigerators
objectives: Derive the Carnot efficiency e = 1 - T_c/T_h from the second law.
Compute efficiency and work output for Otto and Brayton cycles on a PV diagram.
Express the coefficient of performance of a refrigerator and its Carnot limit.
Explain why real engines fall short of Carnot (irreversibility, finite-rate heat flow).
demoIdeas: Carnot and Otto cycles on a PV diagram with efficiency readout.

lessons.title: Free energy and thermodynamic potentials
objectives: Define Helmholtz F = U - TS, enthalpy H = U + PV and Gibbs G = U - TS + PV and state when each is minimised.
Derive dF = -S dT - P dV + mu dN and the other differentials via Legendre transforms.
Derive Maxwell relations from the equality of mixed partial derivatives and use one to evaluate an otherwise inaccessible derivative.
Explain the statement 'free energy is the available work' and 'free energy is the force toward equilibrium'.

readings.title: Free Energy as a Force toward Equilibrium

lessons.title: Phase transformations and chemical equilibrium
objectives: Derive the Clausius-Clapeyron equation from equality of G on both sides of a phase boundary and apply it to estimate a boiling point shift.
Interpret a phase diagram (PT) of a pure substance in terms of minimum G.
Derive the equilibrium condition sum nu_i mu_i = 0 for a reaction and the relationship K = exp(-Delta G degree / RT) for ideal gases.
Connect chemical equilibrium to the partition-function approach you will meet in Unit 5.
demoIdeas: Water phase diagram with draggable point; Clausius-Clapeyron slope along the coexistence curve.

units.title: Boltzmann Statistics and Partition Functions
units.summary: The Boltzmann factor and canonical ensemble, averages, equipartition and Maxwell speeds, and the partition function as the bridge from microscopic spectrum to thermodynamics (the calculation behind q_trans, q_rot, q_vib in physical chemistry).

lessons.title: The Boltzmann factor and the probability of a state
objectives: Derive the Boltzmann factor for a small system in thermal contact with a reservoir from the entropy of the reservoir.
Compute relative populations of two energy levels at a given temperature, for example vibrational and electronic levels or NMR spin states.
Define the partition function Z as the normalisation of the Boltzmann factors.
Compute the thermal occupation of a hydrogen atom's levels and show why excited states are negligible at room temperature.
demoIdeas: Level-population bars for a user-defined set of energy levels as T varies, with live Z.

lessons.title: Average values and the equipartition theorem
objectives: Compute the mean energy of a system from Z via U = -d ln Z / d beta.
Apply this to a two-level system and a harmonic oscillator, obtaining the Planck/Einstein average energy.
Prove the equipartition theorem for quadratic degrees of freedom and state its limits (quantum freeze-out).
Calculate the heat capacity of a two-level system (Schottky anomaly) and identify the peak.
demoIdeas: Heat capacity C(T) of a two-level system and of a harmonic oscillator, with the equipartition limit marked.

lessons.title: The Maxwell speed distribution
objectives: Derive the Maxwell distribution of molecular speeds from the Boltzmann factor and spherical phase-space volume.
Compute the most probable, mean and rms speeds and the fraction of molecules above a given speed.
Estimate effusion rates and apply them to Arrhenius-like thermal activation (fraction of molecules above an energy barrier E_a).

lessons.title: Partition functions and free energy
objectives: Derive F = -kT ln Z and obtain S, P, mu and heat capacity as derivatives of ln Z.
Show that Z for independent distinguishable systems factorises and for identical gas particles carries a 1/N! factor.
Compute Z, F, S and P for the ideal gas, recovering Sackur-Tetrode.
Compute vibrational, rotational and translational partition functions for a diatomic molecule and the associated heat capacity contributions.

lectures.title: Lecture 5: Pressure of an ideal gas and fluctuations
Lecture 6: Weakly interacting gases, heat, and work

demoIdeas: Diatomic gas heat capacity C_V(T): translational, rotational, vibrational steps assembled from partition functions.

units.title: Quantum Statistics: Fermions, Bosons, Photons and Phonons
units.summary: Gibbs factor and the Fermi-Dirac and Bose-Einstein distributions, degenerate Fermi gases (electrons in metals), blackbody radiation, Debye theory of solids and Bose-Einstein condensation.

lessons.title: The Gibbs factor, bosons and fermions
objectives: Derive the Gibbs factor for a system exchanging energy and particles with a reservoir and define the grand partition function.
Derive the Fermi-Dirac and Bose-Einstein distributions for the mean occupation of a single-particle state.
Show that both reduce to the Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution when the occupation is small, and state the condition (n lambda^3 << 1).
Explain the relation between spin, statistics and the occupancy of orbitals; connect to the Pauli principle used in electronic configurations.
demoIdeas: Occupation number vs energy for FD, BE and MB at adjustable mu and T.

lessons.title: Degenerate Fermi gases
objectives: Derive the Fermi energy of a free-electron gas from the density of states and compute it for a metal.
Compute the low-temperature internal energy and heat capacity of a degenerate Fermi gas and explain why C is linear in T.
Estimate the Fermi temperature of electrons in copper and the degeneracy pressure in a white dwarf (order of magnitude).
Describe the density-of-states picture (g(epsilon) ~ sqrt(epsilon) in 3D) and sketch occupation at T = 0 and T > 0.
demoIdeas: Fermi-Dirac occupation smeared around epsilon_F as T rises; shaded excitation region giving the linear heat capacity.

lessons.title: Blackbody radiation
objectives: Derive the Planck distribution for photons in a cavity using the density of states and Bose-Einstein statistics at mu = 0.
Derive Wien's law and the Stefan-Boltzmann law by integrating the Planck spectrum.
Explain the ultraviolet catastrophe from the equipartition result and how quantisation of modes fixes it.
Connect to chemical practice: tungsten lamp spectra and the cosmic microwave background as a 2.7 K blackbody.
demoIdeas: Planck spectrum for adjustable T with the Rayleigh-Jeans curve, Wien peak and total power readout.

lessons.title: The Debye theory of solids
objectives: Derive the Debye model: sound waves as phonons with linear dispersion, a cutoff at the Debye frequency, and the resulting heat capacity.
Obtain the T^3 low-temperature law and the Dulong-Petit high-temperature limit.
Compare Einstein and Debye models and say which fails at low T and why.
Estimate the Debye temperature of diamond versus lead from sound speed and atomic density.
demoIdeas: Heat capacity of solid versus T/T_D comparing Einstein, Debye and Dulong-Petit.

lessons.title: Bose-Einstein condensation
objectives: Derive the critical temperature of an ideal Bose gas from the condition on the number of particles in excited states.
Describe the ground-state occupation below T_c and sketch the heat capacity near T_c.
Explain what the BEC wave-function picture means and give one real example (ultracold atoms, liquid helium).
Contrast what happens to fermions and bosons at the same temperature and density.
demoIdeas: Ground-state fraction vs T/T_c for an ideal Bose gas, with the spatial density of a trapped condensate growing a sharp central peak.

units.title: Interacting Particles and Phase Transitions
units.summary: Virial expansion and van der Waals, the Ising model (exact 1D solution and mean-field approximation), phase coexistence and critical points with Landau theory and critical exponents.

lessons.title: Weakly interacting gases: virial expansion and van der Waals
objectives: Write the virial expansion of the equation of state and relate B_2(T) to the intermolecular potential via the Mayer function.
Compute B_2 for a hard-sphere plus attractive-well potential and obtain the van der Waals equation.
Locate the Boyle temperature and critical point of a van der Waals fluid.
Apply the Maxwell equal-area construction to find coexistence pressure.

lectures.title: Lecture 6: Weakly interacting gases, heat, and work

demoIdeas: van der Waals isotherms with the Maxwell construction: temperature slider reveals the critical point and the coexistence region.

lessons.title: The Ising model and the exact one-dimensional solution
objectives: Define the Ising Hamiltonian and its parameters (J, h) and interpret it as a lattice gas or a cooperative-binding model.
Solve the one-dimensional Ising chain with the transfer-matrix method and obtain the free energy and magnetisation.
Show that the 1D chain has no phase transition at T > 0 and explain the argument via domain-wall entropy.
Run a Metropolis Monte Carlo simulation of a 2D Ising lattice in principle and explain what is estimated.

readings.title: The Ising Model of a Ferromagnet

demoIdeas: 2D Ising Metropolis simulator: temperature slider, lattice picture and magnetisation versus T showing the transition near T_c = 2.269 J/k.

lessons.title: Mean-field theory
objectives: Derive the mean-field self-consistency equation m = tanh(beta(Jzm + h)) for the Ising model.
Find the mean-field critical temperature T_c = zJ/k and the critical behaviour m ~ (T_c - T)^{1/2}.
Compute the mean-field free energy and heat capacity discontinuity.
Explain why mean-field theory fails in low dimensions and where it is reliable.
demoIdeas: Graphical solution of m = tanh(m T_c/T): intersection points changing character as T crosses T_c.

lessons.title: Landau theory and critical exponents
objectives: Write the Landau free energy as a power series in the order parameter and derive the second-order transition.
Compute the mean-field values of the critical exponents alpha, beta, gamma, delta.
Explain first-order transitions in Landau theory (cubic term or negative quartic coefficient).
State what universality means and why exponents depend only on dimension and symmetry, linking to the van der Waals critical point.
demoIdeas: Landau free energy versus order parameter: sliders for a(T-T_c) and cubic term, minimum position tracing the transition.

units.title: Ensembles and Fluctuations
units.summary: The formal structure behind everything above: microcanonical, canonical and grand canonical ensembles, why they agree in the thermodynamic limit, fluctuations and response functions, classical gases and the cluster expansion.

lessons.title: Probability, the central limit theorem and the thermodynamic limit
objectives: Compute means, variances and cumulants of discrete and continuous distributions, including the Poisson and Gaussian.
State the central limit theorem and use it to show that relative fluctuations of extensive quantities scale as 1/sqrt(N).
Explain why this makes ensembles equivalent for macroscopic systems.
demoIdeas: Sum of N random variables: histogram converging to a Gaussian with the width shrinking as 1/sqrt(N).

lessons.title: Microcanonical, canonical and grand canonical ensembles
objectives: Define the microcanonical ensemble and entropy S = k ln Omega, and derive the canonical ensemble by coupling to a bath.
Define the grand canonical ensemble and derive the grand potential Phi = -kT ln Z_G.
Express the thermodynamic quantities (U, S, P, mu) in each ensemble and show how they are related via Legendre transforms.
Choose the appropriate ensemble for a given problem (fixed N,V,E; fixed T; open system).

lessons.title: Fluctuations and response functions
objectives: Derive energy fluctuations in the canonical ensemble, Var(E) = kT^2 C_V.
Derive number fluctuations in the grand canonical ensemble and relate them to the compressibility.
State the fluctuation-dissipation idea: equilibrium fluctuations determine linear response coefficients.
Explain the divergence of fluctuations at critical points (critical opalescence).

lectures.title: Lecture 5: Pressure of an ideal gas and fluctuations

demoIdeas: Small-system canonical simulation: energy histogram width versus T and N compared with kT^2 C_V.

lessons.title: Classical gases: Gibbs paradox, cluster expansion and Debye-Huckel
objectives: Write the classical partition function for an interacting gas as a phase-space integral and explain the 1/N! and h^3N factors.
Derive the cluster expansion to second order and recover the virial coefficients.
Describe the Debye-Huckel treatment of electrolytes, derive the Debye screening length and relate it to ionic strength in solution chemistry.
Use the Maxwell distribution and equipartition to obtain classical heat capacities and see where the classical results fail.
